title: Exploring living kingdoms
summary: Practise grouping animals, plants, fungi and microorganisms by their main features.
keyIdeas: This topic uses a school model of five kingdoms to group living things. Other classification systems also exist.
Animals and fungi do not make their own food. Plants generally make food using sunlight.
Vertebrates have a backbone. Invertebrates do not.

basicKnowledge: A. Cultura científica › La vida en nuestro planeta
A. Cultura científica › Iniciación en la actividad científica

activities.prompt: Classify these living things by kingdom.
activities.explanation: These plants make their own food and remain rooted in place. These animals feed on other organisms and move around.

activities.prompt: Mushrooms belong to the plant kingdom because they grow from the ground.
activities.explanation: Mushrooms belong to the fungi kingdom. Unlike plants, fungi cannot make food through photosynthesis.

activities.prompt: Aisha examines yoghurt through a microscope and finds tiny living things made of one cell. What are they?
activities.explanation: Yoghurt contains helpful bacteria: single-celled microorganisms in the bacteria group of this school model.
activities.hint: They are microscopic living things made of a single cell.

activities.prompt: Match each vertebrate group to a common feature.
activities.explanation: Vertebrate groups have characteristic coverings and ways of breathing suited to their environments.

pairs.right: Hair or fur, and young fed with milk
Dry skin covered in tough scales

activities.prompt: Adrián says aquarium corals are plants because they stay attached to rocks. What is his mistake?
activities.explanation: Corals are animals that capture food from water. Many also live with algae that photosynthesise.
activities.hint: How do they obtain food and energy?
options: They are animals, even though they stay attached and capture food from water.
They are sea fungi that absorb salt from the seabed.
They are magical rocks that grow in salt water.

activities.prompt: Complete the sentence about fungi's nutrition.
activities.explanation: Some fungi break down dead material. Others interact with living organisms in different ways.
activities.sentence: Some soil fungi obtain nutrients from dead leaves through ___.

activities.prompt: Wei sees a fern with roots and green leaves making food using light. Which group does it belong to?
activities.explanation: A fern is a plant. Some algae and bacteria also photosynthesise, so photosynthesis alone does not uniquely identify plants.
activities.hint: Recall which group ferns belong to.
options: A green plant-eating animal that does not move.
A fungus that needs sunlight to warm up.
A plant that uses sunlight to make its food.

activities.prompt: Classify these animals by whether they have a backbone.
activities.explanation: Vertebrates have a backbone. Invertebrates do not, although some have hard protective structures.

activities.prompt: Read Omar and Martina's laboratory experience and answer the questions.
activities.explanation: The tiny protozoa in this example are single-celled organisms living in water, observed with a microscope.
activities.title: A drop full of life
activities.text: Omar and Martina collect a drop of still water from the school pond. With their teacher's help, they place it on a slide and look through a microscope. At first they see only clear water, then tiny swimming creatures appear. Omar spots an amoeba changing shape to catch particles. Martina finds elongated paramecia covered in tiny hair-like structures called cilia. Their teacher explains that these are single-celled microorganisms. In the school classification model, they are protozoa, rather than plants or animals.

questions.prompt: Which instrument do they need to see these living things?
questions.explanation: The text says they examine the drop with a school microscope.

questions.prompt: Why could they not see the amoebas with their unaided eyes?
questions.explanation: These microorganisms are so small that magnifying lenses are needed to distinguish them.
options: They are microscopic single-celled organisms, too small to see with unaided eyes.
They hide inside stones at the pond bottom.
They swim only when the room is completely dark.

activities.prompt: Order the steps for classifying an organism with a guide.
activities.explanation: Observe and compare evidence before classifying. Naming a newly discovered species requires specialist work.
items: Observe its features without harming it.
Use the guide to learn about its body and how it feeds.
Compare the evidence with groups in the guide.
Record the classification and reasons for it.
